item.title: 94 mil reproducciones · 1346 reacciones | New cat alert! A call from a wildlife sanctuary about a "weird cat" has led to the first new cat species discovered in over 100 years. Smaller than an average housecat and covered in leopard-like spots, the cat species—proposed name Leopardus tilcayo—lives in Bolivia’s Yungas forest ecoregion, and very little is known about its day-to-day life in the wild. Its discovery is redrawing the branches of the cat family tree, and researchers hope the methods used to identify it could be used to find even more new cat species around the world: https://on.natgeo.com/INjRv5 | National Geographic

item.description: Astronaut training is so much more than learning how to fly in space geology, survival, teamwork, and problem-solving all matter. It’s amazing to see the preparation behind the people who may explore worlds beyond Earth. Curious Science Lab Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Curious Science Lab I've discovered that outer space, which I call "the lower heavens," is spherical like the Earth. What do you think of this discovery? I have more discoveries…
item.description: Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Real-time quantum jump in sound observed for first time
item.description: A Stanford team has documented the first direct observation of quantum jumps of sound in a mechanical resonator, completing an arc of scientific exploration that started more than 100 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Virtual biotech company puts thousands of AI scientist agents to work on drug discovery
item.description: The latest company to spin out of a Stanford Medicine lab is a biotech undertaking with 37,000 employees—and none of them are human. There's no lab space, no lunch breaks and no payroll. It's an artificial intelligence-powered virtual biotech company that's the brainchild of associate professor of biomedical data science James Zou, Ph.D., who is also the principal investigator of a virtual lab that launched in 2025, and graduate student Harrison Zhang. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US sanctions boost China’s science-driven innovation by over 70%, study finds
item.description: Sanctioned Chinese companies are increasingly turning to open-source research to innovate and reverse-engineer restricted foreign technology, with a 72 per cent surge in scientific literature citations in their patent applications, according to a new study. While the United States said it expanded its Entity List to safeguard national security and preserve its technological edge, an analysis of Chinese patent filings over the 12 years until 2022 showed that US restrictions on access to... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Holly Chik

item.title: Why the places we love in books can never quite be found in real life
item.description: From the Brontës' Haworth to Jane Austen's Bath, Wordsworth's Lake District and Thomas Hardy's Dorset, literary places continue to exert a powerful hold over readers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marine carbon dioxide removal is advancing, but questions remain about viability, says new digital report
item.description: Marine carbon dioxide removal (CDR) has advanced significantly, with growing research activity, technological development, private-sector involvement and movement toward field testing. But major questions remain about whether these approaches can remove carbon dioxide at meaningful scales, how that removal can be reliably measured and verified, potential environmental effects, and how marine CDR should be governed, says a new digital report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a simple game of 20 questions could help make AI fit for the future
item.description: Artificial intelligence programs used to classify images could be trained much more cheaply using a surprisingly simple method inspired by the childhood game of 20 Questions, according to new research posted to the arXiv preprint server by a team from the University of Bristol. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nullarbor mapping reveals surface signs of deep, hidden cave systems
item.description: Mysterious trenches stretching for kilometers across southern Australia's Nullarbor Plain have been revealed as the surface footprints of deep, hidden ancient cave systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study maps where humans drive harmful nutrient levels along coasts
item.description: Along a quarter of the planet's coastal waterways, humans contribute more harmful nitrogen—via agricultural runoff, wastewater discharges and other activities—than all natural sources combined. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New benchmark puts quantum computers to the test and reveals their limitations
item.description: Quantum computers are no longer theoretical concepts. Today, they are being developed to tackle a range of complex problems, including exploring financial risk, modeling complex molecules and optimizing massive logistics networks. However, until now, there has been no way to benchmark the computational power of different systems on the same scale to see how they compare. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What ancient Mars rocks reveal about its buried carbonate stores
item.description: Carbonate minerals are among the best records of past liquid water on Mars: They form when water carrying dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with rock, and their composition reflects the chemistry of both. Yet Mars has surprisingly little carbonate on its surface compared with what climate models predict, given that the planet likely had a (at least transiently) thick, CO2-rich atmosphere more than 3 billion years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Opt-out AI training plan could weaken Australian copyright protections
item.description: The ground is shifting beneath the feet of Australian authors and other creatives. A leaked proposal seen by the ABC suggests the government might grant artificial intelligence (AI) companies access to the copyrighted works of Australians under an opt-out system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sixteen new fungus species found hiding in Thailand's flowers
item.description: Researchers have discovered 16 new species of fungus living unnoticed inside garden flowers and wildflowers across northern Thailand, more than quintupling the number of such fungi known to occur in the country. The findings are published in the journal IMA Fungus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Capybaras in the desert? Fossil casts doubt on Atacama as world's oldest continuously dry region
item.description: Ask any zoo-goer and they will tell you that capybaras are adorable. Ask a scientist specializing in the rodents, which resemble oversized guinea pigs, and they will tell you they are obligate semiaquatic herbivores that indicate persistent riparian ecosystems. In plain English: Capybaras like it wet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea hydrothermal vents may be a hot spot for pregnant Antarctic krill
item.description: Antarctic krill are tiny shrimp-like creatures that were previously thought to mostly inhabit the upper layer of the Southern Ocean. Although they had occasionally been observed at deeper levels, they were never seen near deep-sea hydrothermal vents until 2024, when a group of oceanographers observed them there for the first time. The team's new study, published in Communications Biology, describes the discovery and why the team thinks pregnant krill may actually be spending a lot of time near hydrothermal vents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why does laundry get smelly if it stays wet? A textile scientist explains how to fix it
item.description: You forget a load in the machine overnight, and by morning it smells worse than before you washed it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La órbita terrestre es un basurero: 17.000 toneladas de chatarra rodean la Tierra
item.description: La Agencia Espacial Europea contabilizó al 31 de julio, 46.870 objetos artificiales en órbita "detectables". Es decir, hay muchos más. Hay unos 230 millones de fragmentos de menos de un centímetro, que -a la velocidad que vuelan- son un peligro. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: Japanese supercomputer simulations may explain Webb's Little Red Dots
item.description: Of all the discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope, the multitude of Little Red Dots it has observed is among the most enigmatic. Now, simulations using the Japanese Supercomputer ATERUI III have explained the nature of the Little Red Dots without requiring any exotic assumptions. The simulations show that the Little Red Dots are black holes growing at a rate that would be impossible today because of conditions in the early universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European ash pangenome could help researchers breed a generation of trees resistant to ash dieback
item.description: In a study published in the journal Nature Communications, researchers from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Forest Research and collaborating organizations present the first-ever European ash (Fraxinus excelsior) pangenome, using high-quality DNA to aid research into natural ash dieback resistance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diamond quantum sensors can detect heart magnetism at room temperature without skin contact
item.description: Physicists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) have developed a technology that uses quantum sensors to measure biomagnetic signals, such as heart activity. Researchers from the DIAQNOS (DIAmond-based Quantum Sensing for NeurOSurgery) flagship project, coordinated by Dr. Arne Wickenbrock in Mainz, have demonstrated the potential of quantum technology for future medical applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Education reform student and professor find that social media also affects students in developing countries
item.description: Sometimes the best collaborations start with disagreements in class discussions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Black holes from stellar to supermassive size may follow one jet-launching rule
item.description: An early-career Western Australian astrophysicist has helped uncover a universal rule behind one of the most powerful behaviors in the universe: when black holes launch jets. The discovery, published in the journal Nature Astronomy, shows black holes appear to fire off powerful jets at the same critical point in their feeding cycle—whether they are about 10 times the mass of the sun or millions of times heavier. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Unveils Enterprise, the First Space Shuttle
item.description: Fifty years ago, on Sept. 17, 1976—Constitution Day of America’s bicentennial year—NASA unveiled its first space shuttle orbiter, OV-101, to the public. NASA had originally planned to name the vehicle Constitution, but a letter-writing campaign changed the agency’s plans. Nearly 100,000 fans of the Star Trek television series wrote the White House urging that the […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: El Niño may lift Australian food prices as dry conditions squeeze farms
item.description: Australia's farm sector currently faces a double whammy from weather and nonweather-related factors: a confirmed El Niño effect and surging inflationary pressures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild honeybee populations in the EU are on the Red List for the first time
item.description: Populations of the Western honeybee (Apis mellifera) are under immense pressure in the wild in Europe. New research published in Conservation Science and Practice from the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart and Agroscope in Zürich shows that there are frequent occurrences of honeybees in the wild in Europe. However, the researchers estimate that the populations of these bee populations in the European Union (EU) will fall by about 56% within 10 years without the influx of swarms from beekeepers. Therefore, wild honeybees are now officially classified as "endangered" across the EU on the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nebraskans wary of risks surrounding artificial intelligence
item.description: Americans are grappling with artificial intelligence—from its lightning-fast development to the construction of data centers to support it—and are becoming more skeptical of its benefits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Endurance running or endurance diving—which came first?
item.description: A new study combines paleoanthropology and diving physiology to address a fundamental question in human evolution: Why did humans evolve their exceptional aerobic endurance? Did our ancestors begin endurance running to exhaust terrestrial prey, or did breath-hold diving for aquatic resources also play a key role? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea crustaceans caught hitching rides on giant sea spiders
item.description: Some types of marine life appear to have it easy. While exploring thousands of meters below the waves in the Chilean Margin in the southeastern Pacific Ocean, scientists observed tiny shrimp-like crustaceans known as amphipods (Mesopleustes abyssorum) clinging tightly to much larger giant sea spiders (Colossendeis colossea) that were scuttling on the ocean floor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This popular fermented food may help flush nanoplastics from the body
item.description: A kimchi-derived bacterium can bind to nanoplastics under gut-like conditions and may help carry them out of the body. In mice, the probiotic more than doubled the amount of nanoplastics detected in feces, pointing to a surprising potential use for microbes from fermented foods. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: AI is shaping kids. What if kids could shape AI, too?
item.description: Vanderbilt University's Golnaz Arastoopour Irgens, assistant professor of human-centered learning technologies at Peabody College of Education and Human Development, partnered with Sarah K. Burriss (Ph.D. '23, Peabody's Department of Teaching and Learning), assistant professor of the practice at the College of Connected Computing, to rethink how kids should learn about artificial intelligence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Robotic lab sets up and runs optics experiments on demand
item.description: Every new generation of phone display, television screen and solar panel is the result of precision optics experiments, which use lasers and other light sources to measure the optical properties of candidate materials. These experiments can take months to run, requiring scientists to meticulously angle and adjust delicate light sources, mirrors, cameras and other components in a process of careful, constant tuning that can be physically tedious and time-consuming. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japón no ha hecho tanto ruido como la NASA con DART, pero su Hayabusa 2 lleva tiempo ensayando cómo defender la Tierra de un asteroide
item.description: Se habla mucho sobre el papel de la misión DART , de la NASA, en el ensayo de técnicas dirigidas a la defensa planetaria. Sin embargo, otras compañías a las que quizás se ha dado menos publicidad han emprendido misiones similares. Es, por ejemplo, el caso de la Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) con la misión Hera . Ahora, además, Japón se ha unido a la lista con una misión que, en realidad, se concibió con un fin distinto. Y es que, una vez terminada la recogida de muestras del asteroide Ryugu, la misión japonesa Hayabusa 2 ha emprendido un viaje por otros asteroides cercanos, llevando a cabo… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: A $100 detector can see invisible particles raining down from space
item.description: A pocket-sized, roughly $100 detector can reveal the invisible stream of cosmic particles constantly passing through Earth and even through our bodies. What began as a student physics project is now being used in major experiments, balloon missions, and potentially future spacecraft. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Laser scans reveal 23 hidden ship carvings on Bronze Age temple wall in Cyprus
item.description: About 40 years ago, researchers found ancient ship carvings on a temple wall in Cyprus, possibly all carved at once at the tail end of the Bronze Age, around the time of the infamous Bronze Age collapse. Then, decades later, a new study revealed they had missed nearly two dozen ancient carvings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What major tests like PISA and NAPLAN get wrong about Indigenous students
item.description: We've just received the results of the latest PISA test—the international assessment of 15-year-olds' science, math and reading skills. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronomers just found the youngest known planet ever
item.description: Astronomers have confirmed a Jupiter-size planet less than a million years old, making Elias 2-24 b the youngest known planet and giving scientists a rare look at a world still being born. Its surprisingly rapid formation challenges leading theories about how giant planets come together, especially so far from their stars. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: More short holidays close to home boost well-being, study finds
item.description: Travel plays a far more critical role in mental health and well-being than previously thought, according to new University of the Sunshine Coast-led research. The study found frequent leisure travel boosts happiness, psychological resilience and overall quality of life, with the greatest benefits experienced by people who feel vulnerable or struggle to manage stress. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genome assembly of rice stink bug offers new data-informed tool in fight against costly pest
item.description: Scientists are getting a leg up on the rice stink bug, one of the most significant threats to rice, a staple food for nearly half the world's population and a major crop in Arkansas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST’s mysterious little red dots may be black holes growing at incredible speeds
item.description: New supercomputer simulations suggest JWST’s puzzling Little Red Dots are rapidly growing black holes from the early Universe. Extreme radiation may have helped create unusually massive black hole seeds, while dense surrounding gas allowed them to grow dozens of times faster than black holes can today. The simulated objects closely resemble the Little Red Dots seen by Webb. If correct, they could solve the mystery of how enormous black holes formed so soon after the Big Bang. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: At-risk gamers gambling with their financial future
item.description: Nearly 8 out of every 10 people at risk of gaming disorder have experienced overspending or financial harm due to their habit, an international study led by University of Queensland researchers found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Birds basking in natural 'saunas'
item.description: New research led by the University of Otago—Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka shows some bird species may be taking advantage of natural geothermal "health spas." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New livestream brings remote Australian arid zone waterhole to the world
item.description: A new livestream from a remote waterhole in the Northern Territory is giving people around the world the opportunity to observe wildlife in real time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Political boot camps for women could redress gender imbalance
item.description: Immersive boot camps for women could be a way to overcome the stark gender imbalance in political leadership, according to new research that examined how to increase the political ambitions of talented women. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cuttlefish suckers reveal how they grip rough prey—and could inspire better technology
item.description: Cephalopods are a group of soft-bodied marine mollusks that include cuttlefish, octopuses, squid and nautiluses. Many of these mollusks have muscular suckers on their arms that allow them to seize prey or grip other surfaces in their surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Urban fire risk rises 30% in higher-income neighborhoods, analysis finds
item.description: Frequently located on hillsides and in canyons surrounded by wildlands, wealthy neighborhoods are more likely to catch fire. However, a UC Riverside study shows they are also likely to recover faster than lower-income areas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dungeons & Dragons study rolls for better well-being
item.description: Rolling dice and battling imaginary monsters might seem an unlikely source of well-being, but Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) research suggests Dungeons & Dragons groups can provide meaningful social connections and a strong sense of belonging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find a natural gut compound that helps heal the intestine
item.description: A natural compound produced by gut bacteria after digesting foods such as pomegranates, walnuts, and berries may help repair and protect the intestinal lining. The discovery reveals a surprising beneficial side of an inflammatory pathway and could inspire more targeted treatments for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study challenges estimates used to guide Atlantic menhaden fishing
item.description: Atlantic menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus), which supports a major commercial fishery along the U.S. East Coast and serves as essential prey for fish, seabirds and marine mammals, may be less able to sustain fishing pressure than some assessments suggest. A new study finds that a key estimate of deaths from natural causes was substantially overstated, potentially making the population appear more productive than its biology supports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
item.description: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: World's water cycle becoming more unpredictable, UN warns
item.description: The planet's water cycle is becoming increasingly erratic, swinging between too little and too much, the United Nations warned Thursday, with an unprecedented El Niño expected to exacerbate the long-term trend. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA spacecraft discovers a huge new crater on the moon
item.description: Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ESA starts next phase of IRIS² evolution through Low-LEO activities
item.description: The European Space Agency (ESA) has signed 18 consolidation contracts bringing together nearly 80 companies to study new secure and resilient connectivity services. The contracts also cover associated mission concepts and aim to shape the future of the EU's secure connectivity constellation – IRIS² – which will provide Europeans with resilient communications, when and where it matters most. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: NASA scientist's chance Moon discovery reveals once-in-a-lifetime crater
item.description: Wider and about as deep as the Roman Colosseum, researchers believe the newly-discovered McGetchin crater was formed after a powerful surface impact in 2024. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Three space companies win ESA awards for excellence and innovation
item.description: On 16 September at its Industry Space Days 2026 event at ESA–ESTEC in the Netherlands, the European Space Agency (ESA) honoured three space companies with this year’s prestigious awards for excellence and innovation. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Does AI make us smarter or more dependent?
item.description: Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming part of how people learn, solve problems and construct knowledge. Yet whether AI strengthens human intelligence or encourages excessive dependence remains an open question. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Galileo's first civil authenticated position fix under spoofing conditions
item.description: For two hours on the afternoon of Wednesday 16 September, five operational Galileo satellites broadcasting over Europe transmitted a new encrypted signal for testing. On the ground in Andøya, Norway, and at ESA’s navigation laboratory at ESTEC, in the Netherlands, receivers successfully established their location using these encrypted signals, marking the first real-world positioning using Galileo’s upcoming Signal Authentication Service (SAS). Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Remote waterhole live stream a window into secrets of NT desert
item.description: A camera streaming around the clock from a remote Central Australian waterhole is capturing dingoes, wallabies, birds and other wildlife while helping researchers understand how the changing climate is reshaping the desert. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Scientists removed kangaroo rats for 13 years to reveal their hidden role in desert vegetation
item.description: Researchers conducted a thirteen-year investigation by excluding kangaroo rats from designated desert areas. The absence of these rodents led to a remarkable uptick in two specific grass species due to reduced soil disruption and seed predation. This transformation in plant life further influenced the activities of other rodents and foraging birds, effectively highlighting the indispensable role kangaroo rats play in the dynamics of desert vegetation communities. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Former Australian miner spotted Saturn ripple in 2024; two years later, co-authored 10-sided wave
item.description: An Australian amateur astronomer made a groundbreaking observation in their backyard, discovering a colossal ten-sided atmospheric wave. This unique finding corroborated the existence of a decagon around Saturn's south pole, as confirmed by years of data from the Hubble Space Telescope. The decagon, intertwined with fierce jet streams, spans numerous atmospheric levels, shedding light on the circulatory processes within the atmospheres of these gas giants. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: New mesothelioma drug turns cancer’s own defenses against it
item.description: Scientists are testing a counterintuitive way to fight mesothelioma, an aggressive asbestos-linked cancer with few effective treatments. A new experimental mesothelioma drug kills cancer cells by disabling PRX3, an antioxidant defense that tumors use to survive intense oxidative stress. In an early clinical trial, it controlled disease progression in 67% of patients and produced encouraging survival results, raising hopes that the strategy could eventually be used against other cancers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Hong Kong to support rocket, satellite IPOs as SpaceX-led sector takes off
item.description: Hong Kong aims to adjust listing rules to grab a share of initial public offerings (IPOs) by mainland China’s space companies as activity in the sector increases in line with Beijing’s priorities and heightened activity in the sector following the blockbuster June listing by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. That could lead to more head-to-head competition between the Hong Kong stock exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange, which is now drawing a majority of such listing applications, including commercial... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Zoe SL Chan

item.title: NASA finds a 'once in a century' lunar crater, bigger than the Roman Colosseum
item.description: Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: NASA’s New Horizons spots signs of liquid nitrogen flowing on Pluto
item.description: Scientists have found the first evidence that liquid may have flowed across Pluto’s surface in the recent past. Dark features on the enormous Sputnik Planitia glacier appear consistent with liquid nitrogen rising through cracks from deep beneath the ice. Computer models show that nitrogen could melt at the glacier’s base and travel upward like fluid through small conduits. The finding reveals that Pluto may be much more geologically active than its frozen appearance suggests. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Summer Goes Out With a Heat Dome
item.description: Temperature records toppled across the central and southern U.S. as the autumnal equinox approached. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists find a hidden health advantage in black and green rice
item.description: Scientists found that black and green Japanese rice contain unusual, potentially beneficial fats and may be digested more slowly than ordinary white rice. The combination could make these colorful varieties promising ingredients for foods designed to support blood sugar and metabolic health. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: What the Bayeux tapestry reveals about medieval buildings on both sides of the Channel
item.description: For many, the Bayeux Tapestry conjures images of clinker-built ships, prancing horses, the Normans feasting on chicken on the eve of the Battle of Hastings, and the arrow in King Harold's eye that ended centuries of Anglo-Saxon rule. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden “immune organ” in the skull may help fight brain cancer
item.description: Scientists discovered a hidden “immune organ” inside the skull that acts as a rapid first responder against brain cancer in mice. Strengthening this local immune defense improved tumor rejection and survival, raising the possibility of new treatments that target the skull directly. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Tracking visits to public points of interest can inform community health measures
item.description: It's not so much where people live, but where they frequently spend their time, that can provide useful information for predicting community health measures. A team led by geographers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences found that adding place visitation data—geographic data points collected from millions of anonymous cellphone users with GPS-enabled devices—to a population health model increased the model's predictive performance by an average of 7.5%. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sharks on the move expose the need for international conservation efforts
item.description: Understanding the migration pathways of sharks and rays is key to conserving some of the world's most endangered marine species, according to new University of Queensland research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Survey reveals significant gap across 64 countries between commitment to the rule of law and its implementation
item.description: A new report by the International Bar Association (IBA) has found a significant gap between the importance legal professionals attach to fundamental rule of law principles and their assessment of how effectively those principles are implemented in practice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forest structure matters more than topography in shaping plant diversity in Southern Apennine old-growth forests
item.description: A study in Pollino National Park shows that large trees, complex canopies and deadwood diversity play a major role in shaping vascular plant communities, highlighting the ecological value of one of Italy's most remarkable old-growth forest landscapes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02911-9 Using a video game involving bombs and treasure chests, researchers show how neural activity flickers between two regions of the frontal cortex when the brain weighs up a tricky decision. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Long-term oyster reef restoration shows clear success in murky waters
item.description: Large-scale oyster reef restoration in the Chesapeake Bay is successfully creating three-dimensional habitats that support larger, more diverse fish communities, according to new research from scientists at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The study, published in Ecosphere, provides compelling evidence that restoration efforts are shifting underwater ecosystems from communities dominated by small, transient schooling fish to those supporting larger, resident… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Device simulates natural conditions to grow biofilms and test their antibiotic susceptibility more accurately
item.description: Biofilms are complex microbial communities that adhere to a surface and encase themselves in a viscous matrix they produce. This structure protects bacteria from antibiotics and the immune system far more effectively than if they lived in a free-floating state, making biofilms one of the most common causes of hard-to-treat chronic infections—such as respiratory infections in people with cystic fibrosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), chronic wounds, or infections associated with catheters and prosthetic devices. Added to this is the global rise in antibiotic resistance… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hot electrons reveal electronic collisions may raise resistance in twisted graphene
item.description: When a material heats up, its electrical resistance often rises. The harder question is what, exactly, is getting in the way. The electrons carrying the current may be scattered by vibrations of the material's atomic lattice, known as phonons. They may also collide with one another. Frustratingly, a conventional temperature test warms the electrons and the lattice together, so the effects arrive tangled in the same resistance measurement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Building big with DNA gets a software upgrade
item.description: Forty-four years ago, Nadrian Seeman published his groundbreaking ideas on using DNA as a structural material, expanding DNA's significance far beyond its role as a carrier of genetic information. Since then, the steadily growing field of DNA nanotechnology has seen numerous innovations. One was the DNA origami technique, which enables researchers to fold a single long strand of DNA into a desired 2D or 3D shape. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ChatGPT at university: Study maps why students stick with AI for learning
item.description: What factors influence students' decisions about whether they will continue to use ChatGPT for learning in the future? This was the question addressed by a new study from ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, which used an interpretable machine learning framework to identify the factors that most strongly influence the use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Thinking outside the binding site: Drug molecule makes a square peg fit a round hole
item.description: A square peg doesn't fit a round hole. But what if the peg could change the shape of the hole? A newly developed drug molecule can do something surprisingly similar when binding to its target protein, according to a University at Buffalo-led study published Tuesday (Sept. 15) in Angewandte Chemie International Edition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Henry VIII's dissolution enforcer stashed Catholic manuscript—its lost pages have just been rediscovered
item.description: Sir John Gage, a key figure in Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries, saved a dangerous Catholic book from likely destruction, a new study suggests. The identification of six lost pages of a medieval bestseller—illicitly prized by Catholics in the Reformation—as belonging to Gage, exposes the split loyalties of one of Tudor England's great survivors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: It’s fascinating that objects only about twice Jupiter’s mass can form through a star like process yet never ignite hydrogen fusion. Webb keeps showing us that the boundary between planets and stars is much more interesting than we thought. Curious Science Lab Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds
item.description: Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found. Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse , which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3.885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Volatile organic compounds may be underestimated in the carbon cycle
item.description: Rainwater connects the biogeochemical cycles of land and the atmosphere. It's effectively a chemical conveyor belt that delivers compounds to the ground during a process called wet deposition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Insect remains reveal Indigenous burial practices in the Canary Islands
item.description: Archaeologists have analyzed insect remains preserved in the 7th to 9th centuries AD funerary cave of Cruz de la Esquina, Gran Canaria, and found that it was used by the island's Indigenous people for food storage before being adapted into a burial site. The findings have been published in the journal Antiquity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global database reveals hidden diversity and potential of deep-sea microbes
item.description: The ocean's aphotic zone—the dark, high-pressure region below the surface, where sunlight cannot reach—is home to a vast wealth of microbial life. Yet scientists know relatively little about the genetic makeup, growth and function of many of these enigmatic organisms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Brazilian sedge reproduces sexually but without DNA reshuffling, producing genetic clones
item.description: Sexual reproduction usually reshuffles genetic information, creating offspring that differ from their parents. But one small plant takes an unexpected route. In a new study published in Nature, an international team led by André Marques at the Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research in Cologne has shown that the Brazilian beak-sedge Rhynchospora tenuis reproduces sexually—producing pollen, fertilizing its egg cells and setting seeds—but has completely lost the reshuffling of DNA between chromosomes from each parent. The offspring retained the same genetic makeup as their mothers… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bird flu has claimed its first Australian sea lion and dolphin. How does the virus get into these animals?
item.description: A rare Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) on Kangaroo Island has been confirmed to have died from highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu. The sea lion had recently been attacked by a shark, weakening it. Testing revealed that the virus caused its death. Another dead sea lion is being tested. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mobile trap transports 92 antiprotons by road and stores them for over a month in world first
item.description: In March 2026, scientists succeeded in transporting antiprotons by road for the first time in a purpose-built trap loaded on a truck. The BASE collaboration, which realized this experiment at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva under the lead of Professor Dr Stefan Ulmer and Dr Christian Smorra from Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU), now presents its findings and experiences from this pioneering experiment in the journal Nature. Among other things, they report that it was possible to store antiprotons in a mobile transport vessel for more than a month for… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny oyster larvae rely on gravity to feed
item.description: Eastern oyster larvae are only 100–300 micrometers long, but their dense calcium carbonate shells make them substantially heavier than the surrounding seawater. A new study led by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) shows that this excess weight allows gravity to drive the feeding currents the larvae use to bring food to their mouths, a finding that reveals a critical role for gravity in how these tiny animals feed and survive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Simple messaging can help restore trust in US elections
item.description: Election officials can build public trust in procedures and results—even among suspicious voters who fear partisan manipulation—by creating videos that factually explain their security safeguards in simple terms. These are the findings of studies co-authored by a UC Riverside scholar, offering strategies for election officials to respond to false claims and conspiracy theories about election fraud and security, as well as suspicions that arise when mail-in ballot counting delays results. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Compact optical screen could pave the way for cheaper infrared cameras
item.description: New research led by the ARC Center of Excellence for Transformative Meta-Optical Systems (TMOS) at the University of Melbourne demonstrates a new way to make invisible infrared light visible without relying on the expensive detector technology used in today's infrared cameras. Fuente: Phys.org.
